RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the Housing Authority:
  1. Approve the City of Palmdale Housing Authority 2024-25 Annual Report prepared
  pursuant to California Health & Safety Code §34176.1; and,

  2. Direct staff to post the report on the City’s website.

BACKGROUND

The California Health and Safety Code (HSC) requires Housing Successors to prepare
annual reports on the Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund (LMIHAF). These
reports provide the governing body of the Housing Successor with information about the
Housing Successor's activities and housing assets.

The former Redevelopment Agency of the City of Palmdale was dissolved on February
1, 2012. Pursuant to the Dissolution Act, the City Council adopted Resolution No. CC
2012-003 on January 4, 2012, designating the Housing Authority of the City of Palmdale
as the entity responsible for performing the housing functions previously performed by
the Redevelopment Agency, and the Commissioners of the Housing Authority adopted
Resolution No. HA 2012-001, accepting the designation as the entity that would
subsequently perform those housing functions.

Senate Bill 341, effective January 2014, and Assembly Bill 1793, effective January 2015,
amended California Health and Safety Code §34176 and required specified housing
activity and financial information to be provided to the Housing Successor’s legislative
body and posted on its website within six months of the closing of the previous fiscal year
(i.e., on or before December 31st).
 Report to Vice Chair and Commissioners of the Housing Authority
Re: 2024-25 Housing Asset Fund Annual Report
December 2, 2025
Page 2

DISCUSSION

Housing Asset Funds play a critical role in promoting affordable housing development
and preservation throughout California. Established in response to housing crises, these
funds aim to increase the availability of safe and affordable housing options for low-
income residents. As outlined in the 2024-25 Annual Report, the funds are utilized for
various purposes, including new construction, the rehabilitation of existing units, and
support for homeownership programs.

The California Health and Safety Code outlines the framework for managing Housing
Asset Funds, emphasizing compliance, accountability, and transparency. Key provisions
mandate local agencies to report on the use of these funds, ensuring that they align with
broader housing policies and community needs (as is defined by the mandates created
through the dissolution of redevelopment on February 1, 2012). The key requirements
are:

  1. In each 10-year period, no more than 50% of the units that receive LMIHAF
  assistance can be designated as senior citizen units.

  2. In each 5-year period the Successor Housing Agency must demonstrate that at
  least 30% of the LMIHAF expenditure was for the development of housing for
  households earning 30% or less of area median income (AMI) and that no more
  than 20% of the LMIHAF expenditures were for the development of housing for
  households earning between 60% and 80% of AMI.

This regulatory oversight is crucial for ensuring funds are effectively utilized in compliance
with the established requirements. As outlined in the attached Annual Report, the
percentage of LMIHAF units designated as senior citizen units was 23%. In addition, as
reported during the last 5-year cycle, which was included within the 2023-24 Annual
Report, the development of housing within the AMI parameters was distributed as
required. As such, the Housing Successor is in compliance with the requirements relating
to the use of funds.

FISCAL IMPACT

$0; There is no fiscal impact associated with this action.

STRATEGIC PLAN

Goal II: Ensure long-term fiscal health of the City and maintain funding for services.

  C. Involve and expand engagement to enhance public oversight and transparency.

Introduction

California Health & Safety Code §34176.1* requires that each housing successor present
to its legislative body and post on its Internet website an annual report that contains the
following items for the previous fiscal year:

    The amount deposited to the Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund
  distinguishing items listed on the Recognized Obligation Payment Schedule from
  other accounts.
    A statement of the balance in the fund as of the close of the fiscal year,
  distinguishing any amounts held for items listed on the Recognized Obligation
  Payment Schedule from other amounts.
    A description of expenditures from the fund by category, including but not limited
  to, expenditures for:
  o monitoring and preserving the long-term affordability of units subject to
  affordability restrictions or covenants entered into by the redevelopment
  agency or the housing successor and administering activities funded with
  the Low and Moderate Income Housing Asset Fund
  o homeless prevention and rapid rehousing services
  o development of affordable housing.
    The statutory value of real property owned by the housing successor, the value of
  loans and grants receivable, and the sum of these two amounts.
    A description of any transfers made to a contiguous jurisdiction for the purpose of
  developing transit priority projects, permanent supportive housing, housing for
  agricultural employees or special needs housing in the previous fiscal year and, if
  still unencumbered, in earlier fiscal years and a description of and status update
  of any project for which transferred funds have been or will be expended if that
  project has not yet been placed in service.
    A description of any project for which the housing successor receives or holds
  property tax revenue pursuant to the Recognized Obligation Payment Schedule
  and the status of that project.
    For interests in real property acquired by the former redevelopment agency prior
  to February 1, 2012, a status update on compliance with Section 33334.16, as
  amended by Section 34176.1(e). For interests in real property acquired on or after
  February 1, 2012, a status update on the project.
    A description of any outstanding obligations pursuant to Section 33413 that
  remained to transfer to the housing successor on February 1, 2012, of the housing
  successor’s progress in meeting those obligations, and of the housing successors
  plans to meet unmet obligations.
    The housing successor shall include in the report posted on its Internet website
  the implementation plans of the former redevelopment agency.
    If the housing successor fails to comply with the extremely low income requirement
  in any five year report, demonstrate progress to comply in the annual report.
    The percentage of units of deed restricted rental housing restricted to seniors and
  assisted individually or jointly by the housing successor, its former redevelopment
  agency, and its host jurisdiction within the previous 10 years in relation to the
  aggregate number of units of deed restricted rental housing assisted individually

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Receive and file the monthly investment activity reports for October 2025 for the
  City of Palmdale and Successor Agency.

BACKGROUND

Pursuant to Section 16 of the City and Successor Agency Investment Policy, the City
Treasurer shall prepare and present monthly reports on investments to the City
Manager/Executive Director and the City Council/Directors. The reports shall detail the
type of investment, issuer’s name, purchase date, maturity date, amount of deposit, and
interest rate. This information shall be provided for all City and Successor Agency pooled
investments and for Certificates of Participation, Revenue Bonds, Tax Allocation Bonds,
Assessment Districts, and Community Facilities District accounts managed by outside
Fiscal Agents.

The monthly investment reports provide a synopsis of the City and Successor Agency’s
investment activity. They provide information on assets, allocations, average maturities,
yields, and book valuations. The interest rates presented are the most current rates
available as of the date of this report.

The market values presented for pooled City and Successor Agency investments are
based on closing prices for the related investment as of the date of this report. This
information was obtained from the Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg Financial Markets,
Capital Market Finances, or other reliable sources of market prices.

DISCUSSION

Compliance with Investment Policy

For October, the City’s invested portfolio totaled $299,653,846, a decrease of
$4,698,746 from the previous month and $33,824,598 less than the prior year. The
monthly decrease was due to withdrawal from Local Agency Investment Fund (LAIF) to
cover operating expenses for the month.

The par value of the Successor Agency’s portfolio as of October was $10,217,997, an
increase of $75,026 from the prior month due to earned interest.

All investments meet criteria appropriate to Section 8 of the Investment Policy. The
portfolios are based on a combination of various investments, including CDs, Corporate
Notes, US Treasury Securities, and Government Agency Paper, each adhering to
portfolio percentage limitations.

The Finance Division is the custodian for the City and Successor Agency’s investment
portfolio and follows the three main principles of both entities’ investment policies: 1)
Investment in financial instruments that mitigate the risk of monetary losses stemming
from market fluctuations; 2) Establish and maintain a portfolio that has sufficient liquidity
to allow the City and Successor Agency to meet all anticipated cash requirements; and,
3) Seek out investment instruments that provide a competitive market rate of return.

Liquidity

One core approach the Finance Division focuses on is providing liquidity to meet the
City and Successor Agency’s operational requirements. Thus, the City invests in two
pooled funds, the Local Agency Investment Fund (LAIF) and the California Asset
Management Program (CAMP). These are intended for daily operational activities and
can be used during economic uncertainties for ongoing operating and maintenance
needs. The pooled funds provide a higher liquidity ratio, ensuring the City and Successor
Agency meet their cash flow requirements.

The City’s LAIF balance at the end of October was $103,815,128, a decrease of
$4,808,017 from the prior month due to a transfer from LAIF to the City’s general bank
account to cover operational expenditures.

The Successor Agency’s LAIF balance at the end of October was $3,985,613, an
increase of $43,068 from the prior month, due to interest earned.

The City’s CAMP balance at the end of October was $53,729,147 compared to
$53,535,437 in September. The increase is due to interest earned.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the Successor Agency to the Community Redevelopment Agency
of the City of Palmdale:

  1. Adopt Resolution No. SA 2025-004 approving the Recognized Obligation
  Payment Schedule (ROPS 2026-27) for the period of July 1, 2026, through June
  30, 2027; and,

  2. Adopt Resolution No. SA 2025-005 approving the Administrative Budget for the
  Period of July 1, 2026, through June 30, 2027 (Administrative Budget 2026-27).

BACKGROUND

Assembly Bill 1X 26 (AB 26) was signed by the Governor on June 28, 2011, and upheld
as constitutional by the California Supreme Court. On June 27, 2012, the Governor
signed Assembly Bill 1484 (AB 1484). AB 26 and AB 1484 (together the Dissolution
Bills) made sweeping changes to California Redevelopment Law, eliminating
redevelopment agencies statewide, establishing successor agencies, and requiring the
successor agencies to pay, perform, and enforce the enforceable obligations of the
former redevelopment agencies and to wind down the affairs of the former
redevelopment agencies.
 Report to Vice Chair and Directors of the Successor Agency
Re: Adopt Reso Nos.SA 2025-004 and SA 2025-005
December 2, 2025
Page 2

Administrative Budget

Section 34177(j) of the Dissolution Bills requires the Successor Agency to prepare an
Administrative Budget annually and submit it to the Los Angeles County Fifth
Supervisorial District Consolidated Oversight Board for approval.

Section 34177(k) of the Dissolution Bills further requires the Successor Agency to
provide the Los Angeles County Auditor-Controller with the administrative cost
estimates from its approved Administrative Budget to be paid from property tax revenues
deposited in the Redevelopment Property Tax Trust Fund.

Health & Safety Code Section 34171(b)(3) states that commencing July 1, 2016, the
administrative cost allowance shall be up to 3 percent of the actual property tax
distributed to the successor agency by the county auditor-controller in the preceding
fiscal year for payment of approved enforceable obligations, reduced by the successor
agency’s administrative cost allowance and loan repayments made to the city pursuant
to Section 34191.4(b) during the preceding fiscal year, subject to a minimum of
$250,000, unless such amount is reduced by the Oversight Board or by agreement
between the successor agency and the State Department of Finance (“Department of
Finance”). Staff has estimated this amount and allocated it to various Successor Agency
costs as detailed in Exhibit A to Resolution No. SA 2025-005.

Recognized Obligation Payment Schedule (ROPS)

Section 34177(l) of the Dissolution Bills requires the Successor Agency to prepare a
Recognized Obligation Payment Schedule (ROPS) listing the enforceable obligations of
the former Redevelopment Agency annually.

Section 34177(l) further requires that (i) the ROPS shall be submitted to the county
administrative officer, the Los Angeles County Auditor-Controller (Auditor-Controller)
and the State Department of Finance (Department of Finance) at the same time that the
Successor Agency submits the ROPS to the Los Angeles County Fifth Supervisorial
District Consolidated Oversight Board for approval; (ii) the ROPS shall be submitted to
and duly approved by the Los Angeles County Fifth Supervisorial District Consolidated
Oversight Board; (iii) the approved ROPS shall be posted on the Successor Agency’s
website; and (iv) the approved ROPS shall be submitted to the Auditor-Controller, the
State Controller and the State Department of Finance.

Section 34180 of the Dissolution Bills (Section 34180) requires certain successor
agency actions to be approved by the oversight board, including Section 34180(c)
“Setting aside of amounts in reserves as required by indentures, trust indentures, or
similar documents governing the issuance of outstanding redevelopment agency
bonds.” The attached ROPS 2026-27 details amounts in accordance with Section
34180(c).

The attached ROPS 2026-27 also includes an enforceable obligation for the repayment
of the Educational Revenue Augmentation Fund (“ERAF”) and Supplemental
Educational Revenue Augmentation Fund (“SERAF”) loans borrowed from the former
Redevelopment Agency’s Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund.

Senate Bill No. 107 (section 14 of Chapter 325, Statutes of 2015) states that the
Successor Agency’s Oversight Board continues to exist and will only cease to exist after
all of its indebtedness has been repaid, and thus, requires that the City’s Successor
Agency’s Oversight Board approve ROPS 2026-27.

DISCUSSION

The attached Resolution Nos. SA 2025-004 and SA 2025-005 seek approval of the
Recognized Obligation Payment Schedule (ROPS) 2026-27 and the Administrative
Budget 2026-27.

Approval of the ROPS and the Administrative Budget will allow the City to remain in
compliance with AB 26 and AB 1484 (together the Dissolution Bills), and to submit the
information timely to the county administrative officer, the Los Angeles County Auditor-
Controller (Auditor-Controller), and the State Department of Finance (Department of
Finance). Simultaneously, the Successor Agency submits the ROPS to the Los
Angeles County Fifth Supervisorial District Consolidated Oversight Board for approval.

Upon approval from the Los Angeles County Fifth Supervisorial District Consolidated
Oversight Board and the State Department of Finance, the City may then incorporate
the requested administrative budgets and payments from the ROPS into its annual
budget for Fiscal Year 2026-27.

FISCAL IMPACT

The Administrative Budget for the period of July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027 totals
$126,966. These funds will be included in various line items in Program 20 of Fund 460
in the fiscal year 2026-27 budget and are included on the ROPS. These funds will be
used to reimburse the City for its staff hours.

The total payments estimated during the one-year period of ROPS 2026-27 is
$13,777,173, of which $7,787,047 is expected to be funded by Redevelopment Property
Tax Trust Funds (RPTTF) to be received from the Los Angeles County Auditor-Controller
(including Administrative Cost Allowance, $5,363,462 is from reserve balance funds
received in the prior year, and $626,664 is from other funds. Amounts are to be budgeted
in various areas of the Successor Agency and Housing Successor Agency budgets.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve Agreement No. A-9585 with Quest Technology Management for network
  hardware and security services for a total not to exceed amount of $259,855 for a
  term of three years with option to extend two additional one year terms and,

  2. Authorize the Interim City Manager or his designee to execute Agreement A-9585
  with Quest Technology Management, including minimal and/or non-substantial
  changes.

BACKGROUND

The Information Technology (IT) Division is continually working to modernize the City’s
technology infrastructure to improve the reliability, security, and efficiency of its network.
Currently, all City facilities use physical connections that route through City Hall in a
traditional “hub-and-spoke” design. As a result, any disruption at City Hall can impact
network access to City facilities.

As the City adopts more cloud-based applications and remote-access services, the
limitations of this structure have become more significant. To address these challenges,
IT has evaluated modern solutions that combine network connectivity and cybersecurity
within a single cloud-based platform. The industry standard for this model is Secure
Access Service Edge (SASE), which strengthens system resilience and centralizes
security management.
 Report to Mayor Pro Tem and City Council

DISCUSSION

Transitioning to a SASE-based network architecture will improve operational reliability,
enhance public service delivery, and reduce long-term technology costs. Each facility
will utilize its own internet connection instead of routing all network traffic through City
Hall. This distributed model removes the current single point of failure, minimizes the
impact of outages, and improves overall network performance, especially as more
systems move to cloud-hosted platforms.

Following a thorough evaluation of available solutions, staff identified Cato’s SASE
Cloud as the option that best aligns with the City’s long-term modernization strategy
goals. Implementing this architecture supports the City’s cloud-first strategy and
provides a secure, scalable, and resilient foundation for critical public services into the
future.

account. Subsequent years will be proposed through the annual budget process.

  safety/injury illness prevention program assessment for the City of Palmdale, for a
  total not to exceed amount of $150,000 for a term of one (1) year; and,

  2. Authorize the Interim City Manager or his designee to execute Agreement No. A-
  9613 with Citadel EHS, Inc., including minimal and/or non-substantial changes.

BACKGROUND

California Labor Code section 6400 requires employers to provide and maintain
conditions that protect workers from injury and illness, a mandate enforced through the
California Occupational Safety and Health Act and the accompanying Cal/OSHA
regulations. The City , as a public employer in the State of California, has a duty to
provide its employees with a safe and healthful workplace.

To meet these responsibilities, the City must regularly evaluate and update its safety
policies, procedures, and training programs. Ongoing assessment is essential to ensure
compliance with state and federal regulations, respond to emerging workplace risks, and
maintain effective systems for preventing employee injuries and mitigating risk.

DISCUSSION

To support the need for ongoing evaluation, the City issued Request for Proposal (RFP)
No. 26-001-1410 on August 14, 2025. The RFP was released through the PlanetBids
procurement platform and publicly advertised on the City’s website and in the Antelope
Valley Press.

The RFP seeks a comprehensive assessment and gap analysis of the City’s safety
program. This review will examine existing policies, procedures, training practices,
hazard controls, and record-keeping systems. The assessment will also compare the
City’s program to the requirements of the California Labor Code, Title 8 Cal/OSHA
regulations, and relevant Government Code provisions.

The City received five proposals, summarized below:

 Vendor/Consultant  Location
 Citadel EHS, Inc  Valencia, Ca
 Eastern Research Group  Concord, MA
 Ehs International, Inc  Lake Forest, CA
 Leidos Engineering, LLC  San Diego, CA
 Aspen Risk Management Group Inc., a
 Tristar Company  San Diego, CA

A five-member evaluation committee reviewed all submitted proposals using the criteria
outlined in the RFP. Each proposal was scored based on the following factors:

•Project Management and Methodology: Clarity, thoroughness, and feasibility of the
proposed approach for conducting the safety program assessment and gap analysis,
including the timeline, workflow, and quality-control measures.

•Project Initiation: The proposer’s plan for launching the project, including
communication protocols, project scheduling, and the firm’s ability to quickly understand
the City’s operational environment.

•Project Staffing: Qualifications, experience, and availability of key personnel, with
emphasis on technical expertise related to Cal/OSHA compliance and municipal
operations.

•Cost: Overall pricing structure, cost-effectiveness, and alignment with the City’s budget.

Based on the scoring results, the committee determined that Citadel EHS, Inc. submitted
the most responsive and comprehensive proposal, offering a strong technical approach,
highly qualified staff, and competitive pricing.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve Agreement No. A-9636 with Benevate, LLC, for implementation of
  software related to grant management and ongoing grant compliance oversight for
  a total not to exceed amount of $217,000 for three (3) years; and,

  2. Authorize the Interim City Manager or his designee to execute Agreement No. A-
  9636 with Benevate, LLC, including minimal and/or non-substantive changes.

BACKGROUND

Many City projects and Housing Authority programs are funded and supported by a
variety of federal, state, and local grant sources, each with its own unique reporting and
compliance requirements. To meet these obligations, the City currently relies on multiple
outside consultants to manage communication, document preparation, and required
filings. This decentralized approach has proven costly, inefficient, and resource-intensive.

To improve efficiency and strengthen overall grant compliance, the City issued Request
for Proposal (RFP) No. 26-002-7100 seeking a comprehensive software solution capable
of managing the City's and its subrecipients’ compliance and reporting requirements
across all funding sources.

DISCUSSION

RFP No. 26-002-7100 was released in July 2025. Interested firms were required to submit
qualifications and demonstrate their ability to provide full-cycle grant management—from
application through reporting, compliance, and closeout—along with financial oversight,
team coordination, data security, vendor support, FedRAMP certification, access
controls, encryption, third-party security reviews, incident response, and data isolation.

A total of 329 software firms were notified, and the City received eight proposals for
consideration, as summarized below:

 Vendor/Consultant  Location
 Advances Business Software  Plano, TX
 Benevate, LLC. (Neighborly)  Atlanta, GA
 Concourse Tech, Inc.  New York, NY
 Desire Innovations  San Jose, CA
 Dulles Technology Partners, Inc.  Leesburg, VA
 FSH Technology  Philadelphia, PA
 Successmetrics Corp.  Moraga, CA
 Sysintellects  Plano, TX

A three-member evaluation committee reviewed all proposals in accordance with the RFP
criteria. Proposals were scored on:

• Staffing and Management Plan – qualifications of key personnel and proposed
oversight structure;

• Firm Qualifications and Experience – demonstrated ability to provide similar services
for public agencies;

• Technical Proposal – capacity, expertise in grant management software, and ability to
meet RFP requirements; and,

• Cost Proposal – overall value and budget alignment.

After initial scoring, the top two firms were invited to provide software demonstrations.
Based on the full evaluation, the committee selected Benevate, LLC and its Neighborly
Software as the most responsive and comprehensive proposal, offering strong technical
capabilities, qualified staff, and competitive pricing.

Neighborly Software will serve as a centralized grant management and reporting platform,
streamlining communication, tracking, compliance documentation, and internal workflows
for City-administered grant programs.

the cloud services layer is processing tasks, or serverless features are utilized.

  Project; and,

  2. Authorize the Interim City Manager or his designee to file the NOC and release

BACKGROUND

Project No. 904 provided ARAM cape sealing on approximately 605,000 square feet
of local streets located at or near Avenue S and 47th Street East, Avenue S and 52nd
Street East, and Avenue S-8 and 45th Street East. The goal of the project is to extend
the service life of the streets by an additional five to seven years.

ARAM cape seals are a sustainable pavement surface treatment ideal for local streets
in moderately distressed conditions. An additional 55,500 square feet of cul-de-sacs
and intersection stop points received a mill and asphalt-concrete overlay treatment to
provide greater strength for the heavy wheel turning and shear stresses associated
with these areas.

action will accept the public improvements as complete and initiate the City’s release

BACKGROUND

Project No. 911 provided Asphalt Rubber Aggregate Membrane (ARAM) cape sealing,
mill and overlay, slurry sealing, on approximately 2.4 million square feet of local streets.

Street East, received a mill, leveling course, and asphalt overlay treatment to improve
the condition of approximately 208,000 square feet of pavement. Area No. 6 received
a cape seal treatment, along with replacement of the inverted shoulder, for improved
drainage and appearance. The goal of the project is to extend the service life of the
streets by an additional five to seven years.

in moderately distressed conditions. An additional 250,000 square feet of local streets
at various locations received a slurry seal treatment. Within these cape seal and slurry
seal areas, 205,125 square feet of cul-de-sacs and intersection stop points received a
mill and asphalt-concrete overlay treatment to provide greater strength for the wheel
turning and associated shearing stress to the pavement surface.

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that the City Council:

  1. Approve Amended and Restated Purchase and Sale Agreement No. A-9634 with
  AVCC Master, LLC, an affiliate of Covington Investments, LLC, for the sale of
  approximately 233 acres located at the southeast corner of Sierra Highway and
  Avenue M (APN: 3126-022-929); and,

  2. Authorize the Interim City Manager or his designee to execute Agreement No. A-
  9634 with AVCC Master, LLC, including minimal and/or non-substantive
  changes.

BACKGROUND

In October 2021, the City entered into a purchase and sale agreement with Covington
Investments, LLC (Agreement No. A-7575) for the conveyance of approximately 96
acres (considered Phase 1) of City-owned, unimproved property at a purchase price of
$2.25 per square foot. The agreement also included the option for future negotiation at
a purchase price of $3.00 per square foot for Phase 2 (86 acres) and $3.75 per square
foot for Phase 3 (86 acres). Between October 2023 and September 2025, a series of
administrative amendments were implemented, adjusting the boundary of the purchase
phases to coincide with additional sub-phasing of the project, accommodating potential
tenants, and revising milestones related to deliverables and escrow closing.
 Report to Mayor Pro Tem and City Council

On January 22, 2025, the City Council approved the Antelope Valley Commerce Center
Specific Plan and certified the Environmental Impact Report for the subdivision of the
432.9-acre site, which will comprise a master-planned commerce center featuring
industrial, commercial, and open space uses, along with all required on-site and off-site
improvements and infrastructure. The specific plan allowed for a maximum building
footprint of 8,302,536 square feet, comprising 8,241,552 square feet of industrial and
60,984 square feet of commercial uses.

DISCUSSION

Agreement No. A-9634 updates the original purchase and sale agreement to:

    Allow more time for the purchaser to market the site and secure a tenant.
    Provide flexibility in development sequencing to support phased acquisition and
  construction.
    Require that the purchaser sign over the rights to all land use/entitlements, plans,
  studies, and environmental work completed on the project to the City.

Key requirements under the amended and restated agreement are as follows:

    Begin escrow on the first phase of development by June 2027 and actively pursue
  closing within 210 days.
    Start construction within 12 months of closing and complete the first phase within
  24 months of closing.
    Enter into negotiations with the City for the acquisition of subsequent phases
  within specified timelines.

In order to maximize flexibility in phasing sequencing for the build-out of the site, and
accommodate the high cost of regional infrastructure improvements front-loaded on the
project, while ensuring the pricing structure previously agreed-upon remains in place,
the agreement assigns pricing in order of development, utilizing Primary, Secondary,
Tertiary Tract language rather than referencing individual Phases 1 through 4 (now
referenced as A through D). The pricing breakdown is as follows:

    $2.30 per square foot for the Primary Tract
    $3.50 per square foot for the Secondary Tract
    $4.25 per square foot for the remainder of the site

As outlined in the economic summary report prepared in compliance with California
Government Code Sections 52200–52201 for the agreement, the purchase prices
indicated above would not be less than fair market value. The draft agreement
strengthens an existing partnership with the purchaser and supports the City’s economic
development goals of build-out along the Avenue M corridor. Additionally, the project is

SUBJECT:  ANNUAL SELECTION OF MAYOR AND MAYOR PRO TEM

RECOMMENDATION

Staff recommend that Council:

  1. Select a Mayor and Mayor Pro Tem for the 2026 calendar year.

BACKGROUND

On April 1, 2025, the City Council approved Ordinance No. 1655 to establish the annual
selection process for the Mayor and Mayor Pro Tem. The first meeting in December is
designated for appointing a councilmember to serve as Mayor, followed immediately by
the appointment of a councilmember to serve as Mayor Pro Tem.

DISCUSSION

The City Council should act in accordance with its adopted procedure to ensure a definite
and certain City Council leadership.

FISCAL IMPACT

$0; Minor costs related to updating the City’s administrative records and public
materials are expected, and can be absorbed within the existing budget.

STRATEGIC PLAN

Goal II: Ensure long-term fiscal health of the City and maintain funding for services.

  MUNICIPAL CODE AND ADOPTING A NEW SECTION 2.08.010 OF
  TITLE 2 OF THE PALMDALE MUNICIPAL CODE, ESTABLISHING THE
  ANNUAL SELECTION OF MAYOR AND MAYOR PRO TEM BY THE
  MAJORITY VOTE OF THE ENTIRE COUNCIL

  I.  Intent of City Council

  A.  The present municipal code authority as set forth in Section 2.08.010 of
Title 2 of the Palmdale Municipal Code establishes an automatic, district based,
numerical rotation for both the office of Mayor and for Mayor Pro Tem. This structure
removes the proper discretion of the entire City Council as regards the selection of
Mayor and Mayor Pro Tem.

  B.  The City Council desires to annually exercise its discretion, and even from
time to time in the course of the term defined by the calendar year, commencing in
January of each year and terminating at the end of December of that calendar year.

  C.  All legal prerequisites to the adoption of this ordinance have occurred as
required by law, and per Palmdale Municipal Code Sections 1.06.040 through and
including 1.06.070, of Title I.
  II.  Ordinance

NOW THEREFORE, THE CITY COUNCIL OF THE CITY OF PALMDALE DOES
ORDAIN AS FOLLOWS:

  SECTION 1. In all respects as set forth in Part I above of this Ordinance which
are hereby incorporated by reference in their entirety.

  SECTION 2. The presently adopted Section 2.08.010 of Title 2 of the Palmdale
Municipal Code is revoked and rescinded in its entirety, effective upon the effective
date of this Ordinance.

  SECTION 3. A new Section 2.08.010 of Title 2 of the Palmdale Municipal Code,
to read in words and figures as follows; is hereby adopted and will be effective thirty
(30) days after its adoption:
 Ordinance No. 1655
Page 2 of 3

  On an annual basis at the first meeting in December the City Council, by
  majority vote of those in attendance, shall first select a council member to
  serve as Mayor, and immediately thereafter select a council member, by
  majority vote of those in attendance, to serve as Mayor Pro Tem. At the
  pleasure of a majority of the City Council, the City Council may, from time
  to time, replace either or both the Mayor and Mayor Pro Tem. The Mayor
  and Mayor Pro Tem shall not serve consecutive terms.

  SECTION 4. The City Council finds that the adoption and codification of this
Ordinance is not subject to review by the California Environmental Quality Act

direct or reasonably foreseeable indirect change in the physical environment and no

  SECTION 5. If any chapter, article, section, subsection, subdivision, sentence,

person, is for any reason held to be invalid or unconstitutional by the decision of any

remaining portion of this Ordinance or its application to other persons. The City
Council hereby declares that it would have adopted this Ordinance and each chapter,
article, section, subsection, subdivision, sentence, clause, phrase, word, or portion
thereof, irrespective of the fact that any one or more subsections, subdivisions,
